seo.title: SaaS website rebuilds built around how customers buy
seo.description: Rebuild a SaaS marketing site with clearer buyer journeys, a simpler structure, reusable pages, and safer launch checks.

hero.title: Rebuild your SaaS website around how people buy.
hero.summary: Turn a crowded marketing site into clear paths for learning, comparing, and taking action.
fit: Replacing a SaaS site that has grown without a plan
Repositioning the product for a new market
Giving marketing a faster way to ship useful pages
hero.primaryGoal: Help each buyer find the right answer without losing valuable pages during the rebuild.

risks.title: More pages do not always make a better website.
risks.introduction: SaaS sites often grow around team requests instead of buyer needs. A rebuild should remove that friction without losing what works.

items.title: The navigation mirrors the company
items.description: Visitors must understand product teams and internal labels before they can find a useful answer.

items.title: Every page tells the same story
items.description: Use cases, industries, and features repeat generic claims instead of answering different buyer questions.

items.title: The rebuild drops useful demand
items.description: Old comparison pages, guides, and campaign URLs disappear because nobody mapped their value first.

solution.title: Five parts of a useful SaaS rebuild.
solution.introduction: We plan the buyer paths, page system, and launch together. The new design does not have to guess what the old site was doing.

items.title: Map the questions people ask before they buy.
items.description: We separate first-time visitors, active evaluators, and ready buyers. Each group gets a shorter path to the information it needs.
highlights: List the questions behind each visit
Match proof to the buyer's stage
Keep a clear route to the primary action

items.title: Build the navigation around real decisions.
items.description: We group pages by the jobs they do, not the team that requested them. Old and new routes are mapped before the structure changes.
highlights: Use names a new visitor understands

items.title: Reuse strong rules, not generic copy.
items.description: Repeated page types share code, metadata rules, and quality checks. Their message and proof stay specific to the audience.
highlights: Share layout rules across real page families
Keep route copy and metadata together

items.title: Make the next step clear on every page.
items.description: We decide what a visitor should do after each page. Product, pricing, demo, and contact paths are tested as one journey.
highlights: Match the action to the page intent
Test every conversion path end to end

items.title: Verify the rebuilt site before switching traffic.
items.description: We crawl the final environment, compare it with the URL map, and test forms, analytics, canonicals, robots, and the sitemap.
highlights: Check the final domain and redirects

method.title: Rebuild in the order risk appears.
method.introduction: Content and routes come before component volume. That keeps the new system useful after the launch team leaves.

steps.title: Audit demand and content
steps.description: Review buyers, search demand, analytics, sales questions, and the current URL inventory.

steps.title: Plan paths and pages
steps.description: Set the navigation, URL map, page jobs, and conversion routes.

steps.title: Build real page families
steps.description: Finish representative product, use-case, and resource pages before extracting patterns.

steps.title: Switch and watch
steps.description: Test production, launch the redirects, and monitor landing pages and leads.

items.title: Clear buyer paths
items.description: Visitors can move from a question to relevant proof and a useful next step.

items.title: A practical page system
items.description: Marketing can add real page families without copying an entire site or using a block registry.

items.title: A safer switch
items.description: Important URLs, metadata, forms, and analytics have been checked in the final environment.

faq.title: Common questions.
faq.introduction: The choices that usually decide whether a SaaS rebuild stays useful after launch.

items.question: Should we redesign and rewrite at the same time?
items.answer: Usually, yes, but not without an inventory. Keep useful demand and facts, then improve the message and experience around them.

items.question: Do we need a component for every marketing idea?
items.answer: No. Start with route-local composition. Promote a component only after a second real page proves the pattern repeats.

items.question: How do we decide which old pages to keep?
items.answer: Look at their audience, search demand, links, conversions, and role in the buyer journey. Every important URL gets an explicit decision.

items.question: Can marketing still move quickly without a page builder?
items.answer: Yes. Reusable page families, clear tokens, and route-level composition can support fast publishing without turning the whole site into serialized UI.

closing.title: Make the site easier to buy from and easier to run.
closing.description: Plan the buyer journey and the URL map first. Then build a page system that stays clear as the company grows.
